## Executive summary

::: {.verdict}
**Pursue Reid Detmers.** He is a controllable mid-rotation left-hander whose underlying stuff grades well above his surface results, which makes him a fit for a rotation in need. His contact-independent estimators sit a full run below his 4.63 ERA. Signed at \$2.625M for 2026 with control through 2028, Detmers can provide stability for a 2026 playoff push and surplus value for the next two seasons.
:::

## The need

The Atlanta Braves sit atop the NL East at 45-22 with one of the best staff ERAs in baseball. This is their best chance to return to the World Series since they won it in 2021. The rotation has held up despite the early-season losses of Hurston Waldrep and Spencer Schwellenbach, both slated to return. However, relying on that deep into October is risky. The depth behind 2024 Cy Young winner Chris Sale is thin: the next options are unproven prospects like JR Ritchie and veterans like Bryce Elder, Grant Holmes and Martín Pérez, all of whose peripheral statistics suggest regression. Another injury to the group down the stretch could be devastating for Atlanta's championship aspirations.

I screened the trade market for starters whose stuff and peripherals outpace their surface results. Rather than paying the premium for the market's top rental, Tarik Skubal, my screen surfaced Angels LHP Reid Detmers.

## Model summary

Every grade in this report comes from one Stuff+ model that grades each pitch on shape quality and delivery characteristics. The model predicts the run value a pitch should produce and reports it as Stuff+, where 100 is league average and the standard deviation is 10.

The model trains on roughly 3.1 million pitches from 2022 through 2026. Its inputs are velocity, induced vertical and horizontal break, spin rate, spin axis, release height, release side, extension, arm angle, the vertical and horizontal approach angles at the plate, and three fastball-relative differentials. Not all sliders are the same, so I split them into sweeper, gyro and traditional subtypes with k-means on horizontal break, vertical break and fastball velocity gap.

Grades are produced out of fold across five pitcher-level folds, so no pitcher ever trains on his own arsenal. Each pitch is standardized to a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 10 within its subtype, so a 104 slider means the same thing as a 104 curveball.

**Target variable.** The target is expected run value. Realized run value on balls in play is mostly luck, so training on it drags every grade toward the mean. I keep realized run value on the outcomes a pitcher controls (whiffs, called strikes, balls, hit-by-pitch and fouls) and replace the ball-in-play term with expected run value from xwOBA on trackable contact. That way the grade describes the pitch, not the defense behind it.

## The deadline screen

The grade becomes a decision tool when a starter's Stuff+ rank is compared with his results rank. Strong stuff with poor results marks a potential buy-low candidate. Weak stuff with strong results could be due for regression. I used the gap between the two ranks to find trade candidates.

## Reid Detmers

The screen ranks Detmers in the 82nd percentile of starters on stuff but only the 58th on results. That 24-point gap suggests he isn't performing to the quality of his stuff, which makes him a target for optimization and positive regression.

| Pitcher | Stuff+ | Stuff+ percentile | RV/100 percentile | Gap |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Reid Detmers | 102 | 82 | 58 | 24 |

**Overview.** Detmers' four-seam grades out as his weakest regular offering at 100.7 Stuff+, yet it accounts for 44% of his pitches. His slider and curveball grade better and miss the most bats. Lowering fastball usage in favor of more sliders and curveballs is the fastest path to closing his stuff-results gap.

| Pitch | Usage | Velo | IVB | Whiff% | Chase% | Stuff+ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| FF | 44.0% | 94.0 | 17.1 | 18.3 | 23.5 | 100.7 |
| SL | 30.9% | 86.3 | -3.6 | 33.0 | 45.3 | 104.0 |
| CH | 12.1% | 83.4 | 10.9 | 29.2 | 32.4 | 101.1 |
| CU | 10.5% | 72.5 | -14.9 | 39.6 | 28.6 | 102.1 |
| SI | 2.5% | 93.5 | 13.7 | 0.0 | 35.0 | 92.7 |

**Optimization.** At 94 mph with 17.1 inches of induced vertical break, Detmers' fastball is built to beat hitters up in the zone. His heat maps, however, show him leaving it over the middle, particularly to righties. Cutting four-seam usage below 40% against RHH, shifting that usage to the slider and curveball, and locating the four-seam up would help the ride play while still setting up the breaking balls beneath it.

Detmers relies on his slider as his primary out pitch, with far less reliance on his curveball. Yet the curveball posts the highest whiff rate in his arsenal despite being deployed as a strike stealer. It carries a 53% zone rate and a 44.1% CSW, the highest mark of any pitch he throws. Hitters chase it only 28.6% of the time, but that appears to reflect Detmers' intent rather than the physical characteristics of the pitch. Moving the curveball below the zone in two-strike counts can convert more of that whiff ability into actual swings and misses, keeping hitters off his fastball and slider.

**Team control.** Detmers is signed at \$2.625M for 2026 (about \$825,000 owed after the deadline) in his second arbitration year, with control through 2028 before free agency in 2029. At 26 he fits a multi-year window, not a two-month rental. The extra years of control will raise his acquisition cost, but they buy a pitcher who can stabilize Atlanta's rotation for this playoff push and for the next two seasons of its win-now window.

## Acquisition economics

I valued Detmers' remaining control window in surplus value, defined as projected production in dollars minus projected arbitration salary, discounted to present value at 8%. I assumed one WAR is worth \$10M.

Arbitration salaries are driven by traditional counting stats such as innings, wins, ERA and strikeouts, not by underlying pitcher quality like Stuff+. Detmers' 2026 salary is suppressed on two counts. His 2025 platform season came entirely out of the bullpen across 63.2 innings, which held down his 2026 salary. Since returning to the rotation in 2026, he has shown above-average stuff while pacing for career highs in innings, strikeouts and WAR, setting him up for a sizeable raise entering his third arbitration year.

Detmers' raise could resemble Brady Singer's in 2025, when Singer jumped from \$4.85M to \$8.75M in his third time eligible. Singer started more than \$2M ahead of Detmers, though, so any platform-year WAR edge Detmers has over Singer can't justify a raise large enough to overtake him. Other relevant comparables in this section of the third-time-eligible market are Michael King and Trevor Rogers. I project Detmers to earn \$7M in 2027 and \$11M in 2028.

| Year | Salary projection |
|:--|--:|
| 2026 (Arb 2) | \$2.625M |
| 2027 (Arb 3) | \$7M |
| 2028 (Arb 4) | \$11M |

| Year | WAR projection^1^ | Value (\$10M/WAR) | Projected salary | Surplus value | Present value |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2026 | 0.85 | \$8.5M | \$0.8M | \$7.7M | \$7.7M |
| 2027 | 1.9 | \$19.0M | \$7.0M | \$12.0M | \$11.1M |
| 2028 | 2.0 | \$20.0M | \$11M | \$9M | \$7.72M |
| **Total** | **4.75** | | | | **\$26.52M** |

::: {.small .text-muted}
^1^ WAR projections come from FanGraphs' public three-year ZiPS projections.
:::

Based on the table above, Detmers' present-value surplus over his remaining 2.5 years of control is \$26.52 million. Attaching a qualifying offer after the 2028 season would likely net the Braves a Competitive Balance Round A pick (likely a 40 FV player), so I add \$5M, bringing his final surplus value to **\$31.52M**.

Below, I assigned each of the Braves' top prospects a Future Value grade, then applied FanGraphs' prospect valuation framework, scaled to \$10 million per WAR, to convert each FV to a surplus-value dollar figure.

| Player | Position | Future Value | Surplus value |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| Cam Caminiti | LHP | 55 | \$37.8M |
| JR Ritchie | RHP | 55 | \$37.8M |
| Eric Hartman | OF | 55 | \$51.1M |
| Tate Southisene | SS/2B | 50 | \$31.1M |
| Alex Lodise | SS | 50 | \$31.1M |
| Owen Murphy | RHP | 50 | \$23.3M |
| Briggs McKenzie | LHP | 50 | \$23.3M |
| Diego Tornes | OF | 50 | \$31.1M |
| John Gil | SS | 45 | \$8M |
| Garrett Baumann | RHP | 45 | \$6M |

Caminiti, Ritchie and Hartman each exceed Detmers' surplus value on their own, so they should be considered off the table in this deal. Given their age and short professional samples, I would also keep Southisene and Tornes out of a deal for now. The Braves also just committed \$3M to Briggs McKenzie, well over his fourth-round slot value in the 2025 draft, which signals how strongly the organization believes in his talent.

That leaves Atlanta's strongest package as **Owen Murphy and John Gil**, totaling \$31.3M in surplus value. Murphy's proximity to the big leagues greatly reduces his risk, while the Angels get the upside of Gil, who is just 20. Because of scarcity at the deadline, the Braves would likely need to overpay. If they are committed to the acquisition, they could add a high-floor, low-ceiling prospect such as Luis Guanipa (40 FV) for roughly \$5M more in surplus, pushing the package well over the threshold.

## Conclusion

The Braves should acquire Reid Detmers at the trade deadline. His peripheral statistics outperform his realized results, he has stayed healthy so far in 2026, and he remains controllable through 2028.

Owen Murphy and John Gil add up to \$31.3M against Detmers' \$31.52M of surplus, and Atlanta keeps top prospects Cam Caminiti, Eric Hartman and JR Ritchie. Murphy is already performing well in AAA, which reduces his variance and assures the Angels he will be a viable major league pitcher. Gil is only 20 and gives the Angels long-term upside.

Acquiring Detmers lets Atlanta hand meaningful September and October innings to a proven arm who is likely to improve, rather than to unproven depth.
